sf:74197a81d84e45e9a739a439f4b2f0ff.d: **Origin Site**: Kaminaljuyu, Guatemala **Artifact Identification**: Stela 10 **Location Information**: Museo Nacional, Guatemala City **Country**: Guatemala (curated at the Museo Nacional de Arqueología y Etnología) **Description**: Three larger fragments of the "black altar" and one smaller partial fragment area. sf:79859a4ef198428385836d222d9c4e96.n: Roman funeral monument of Mercator, Evora
sf:79859a4ef198428385836d222d9c4e96.d: Roman funeral monument of gray marble dated between the year 151 A.D. and 210 A.D. It belonged to Mercator. In the inscription that still retains on one of its faces we can read: D(is). M(anibus). S(acrum). MERCATOR ANN(orum) XXXII (triginta duorum) VXOR. MARITO MERENTI. POSVIT H(ic). S(itus). E(st). S(it).T(ibi). T(erra). L(evis). The translation according to Encarnação, (1984) would say: “Consecrated to the Manes gods. Here lies Mercator, thirty-two years old. The wife of the deserved husband put. May the earth be light to you”. Mercator could be a slave. The funerary monument is of the Cupa type. It is currently preserved in the Frei Manuel do Cenáculo National Museum (Évora, Portugal). Catalog No. ME1822. ENCARNAÇÃO, José d' - IRCP - Inscrições Romanas do Conventus Pacensis - Subsídios para o estudo da romanização. Coimbra: Inst. Arqueolog. Fac. Letras, 1984, pp. 386-7,767,771. 669 photos from Canon 5D Mk IV. Completely processed in Reality Capture.

sf:7291871b17fe42c294ddb79b81c358dc.d: Excavated at the site of San Andrés near the Olmec center of La Venta in Tabasco, Mexico, this artifact is important, suggesting writing in Mesoamerica began in the La Venta area during the Formative Period (Pohl et al. 2002). Drs. Lori Collins and Travis Doering (University of South Florida Libraries) in cooperation with Dr. Mary Pohl (Florida State University), 3D laser scanned the roller stamp in 2005. Collins and Doering along with 3D Specialist Jorge González (USF), have now digitally “unrolled” and 3D printed the stamp, which dates to c. 500 B.C.E. (Pohl personal communication). New visualizations produced demonstrate how it would have been used in ancient times. These models are being utilized in digital heritage classes at USF and by researchers with FSU (Pohl et al.). The availability for viewing through Sketchfab allows for further use and research.

sf:09223536c8e6410f8d419cb07c0213f4.d: Limestone stela of Intef, son of Ka: Intef is shown standing, receiving an offering from a small male figure who stands in front of him; the positioning of this figure and the scale are very characteristic of the First Intermediate Period. Behind Intef are three female figures, all referred to as his wives, named Mery, Iutu, and Iru. The principal text of the stela, which runs horizontally at the top and then continues vertically at the right side and then in front of the lower parts of the principal figures, is a mixture of offering formulas, important historical information, and phrases that form parts of standard idealized biographical texts. [EA1203](https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/Y_EA1203)

sf:9322535017714f188e5b3c310953afdf.d: An ancient Egyptian funerary cone inscribed with an offering formula for a man named Tjay. The cone dates to the 18th-20th dynasties of the New Kingdom. A textured and un-textured version are presented together here for comparison between the two. The un-textured model was exported with a much higher face count (~800k) compared to the textured version (64k, our normal Sketchfab model size) to preserve detail in the mesh. sf:a7b5a2430107486b998489514eb25ec3.d: Roman thymiaterion with dedication inscription. The incense bowl with serrated rim stands on an altar-shaped base with half-plastic eagles at its corners. The support ring for the bowl is carried by four dolphins pointing downward. The altar shaft is inscribed with the dedicatory inscription of Lucius Messius, a benefactor from the staff of the governor, addressed to "Dominus". Consecrations to Dominus (often accompanied by Domina) are known several times from Dacia and Pannonia, as well as from an altar from Carnuntum. Bronze; h 22,1 cm; dm 18,5 cm Do/mi(no) / f(ier)i / ut pact/us / ius(s)it v/isu L(ucium) M/es(s)ium / m(ilitem) / b(eneficiarium) co(n)s(ularis) / legio(nis) "To make it (i.e., this bronze) to the Lord, as he (i.e., the god) had agreed, he commanded by means of a dream Lucius Messius, the soldier, beneficiarius consularis of the legion." sf:a71f5a375c3e4b1d96157ac78d8e2fc2.n: Inscripción romana con numeral (siglo I d.C.)
sf:a71f5a375c3e4b1d96157ac78d8e2fc2.d: Inscripción hallada casualmente en la campaña de excavaciones de 2016 junto a la calle que discurría al Norte del foro y que daba acceso a El Pueyo de Los Bañales. Pudo pertenecer bien a la señalización de un monumento funerario indicando su extensión en pies (_indicatio pedaturae_) o más verosímilmente su texto deba ponerse en relación con algún proceso constructivo o de cantería cuyo uso se nos escapa. Por el uso de la _L_ como _T_ invertida no sería posterior a época flavia. Roman inscription discovered in 2016 on the road that ran alongside the north of the forum and led to the settlement of El Pueyo of Los Bañales. It could be a sign indicating the size of a nearby funerary monument (_indicatio pedaturae_), but blocks with numbers are more commonly associated with quarries and building processes. Because of the use of _L_ in the shape of an upside-down _T_, the inscription can be dated around the Flavian era. Dimensiones (cm): 20 x 43 x 11

sf:a046788697a84acaae4663dfcfd1b1fa.d: Miliario de arenisca recuperado a mediados del siglo XX por el P. Escalada cerca de San Román de Castiliscar de donde fue llevado al Castillo de Javier y de allí, en los años setenta, al Museo de Navarra. Documenta la participación de otra legión del ejército augústeo, la _VI Victrix_, en la realización de trabajos viarios en la zona entre los años 9 y 3 a. C., y que tanto impacto tuvieron en la integración del territorio de las actuales Cinco Villas en la órbita de Roma. Sandstone milestone found by F. Escalada near San Román of Castilliscar in the 20th century. It was stored in the Castle of Javier and from there it was transferred to the Museum of Navarra in the 1970s. It witnesses the involvement of a second legion, the _VI Victrix_, in various works undertaken in the area between 9-3 BC, thanks to which the region that today is called Cinco Villas was integrated in the Roman territory. Dimensiones (cm): (103) x 47 diam.

sf:b8d3e1125b63456085ed0c2b82b7ae52.d: Bilingual South-Arabian / Aramaic funerary inscription discovered inside the burial chamber of tomb FA-5, Mleiha, Sharjah, UAE. (Overlaet 2018:14 Figure 9, Catalog No. 1). Central panel in south Arabian script, text along the rim in Aramaic. Text reads “Memorial and tomb of Amud son of Gurr son of Ali, inspector of the king of Oman, which built over him his son Amud son of Amud son if Gurr, inspector of the king of Oman.” Dated to either 222/221 or 215/214 BCE. First record evidence of an Oman Kingdom (Overlaet 2018:13). Model of the cast of the original before restoration. 358 photos. Completely processed (aligned, scaled, modeled, cleaned, simplified, unwrapped, textured, meshed) in Reality Capture. B. Overlaet 2018. Mleiha, An Arab Kingdom on the Caravan Trails (Brussels 30.10-30.12.2018). Sharjah: Sharjah Archaeology Authority.

sf:b31e2b52f99e4c2faaf8ec17ae1c4d16.d: The upper right corner of a round-topped limestone stela dating to the Eighteenth Dynasty. On the far right, a man is depicted with his arms raised in adoration. He wears a pleated dress and a wig with curls. The hieroglyphs above his head describe him as adoring and praising Amun, while the column in front identifies him as a scribe. Unfortunately, his name is not preserved. The thicker column in the centre of the stela presents the name and titles of the god Amun-Re, who must have been depicted on the left of the stela. Both occurrences of the name Amun have been erased, a clear indication that this stela dates to before the reign of Akhenaten in the Eighteenth Dynasty.

sf:b90c008d8c1e43c0a2d2a310674f1a13.d: A wooden footboard from a cartonnage case with a black and white Apis Bull painted upon it. The Apis bull wears a uraeus on his head and a red beaded net on his back. The inscription around the bull identifies it as the Apis. It also states that the object was made for the Mistress of the House and Chantress of Amun, Tjesmutperet, daughter of Nespasefy. Anubis is written on the back of the board in black. The Apis Bull was added to the decoration of private coffins and cartonnages from the Twenty-second Dynasty onwards. The object dates to the Third Intermediate Period (c. 1069–715 BC). Part of the collection of Sir Henry Wellcome. On loan to the Egypt Centre since 1971 as part of the distribution of the Wellcome collection.

sf:b300b5f7bfde46fd97d7c15ef25bd07c.d: Round-topped limestone funerary stela, which dates to the Twenty-sixth Dynasty (c. 664–525 BC). The decoration on the front face has been added in black ink, with some traces of red ink for some of the internal details. In the lunette, a winged sun disc is located atop two symmetrical wadjet eyes. In the scene below, two figures (female and male) are shown on the right with their arms raised in adoration before the mummiform figure of Osiris. The lower half of an additional figure, perhaps Isis, is depicted behind Osiris. Beneath the main scene are two horizontal lines of hieroglyphs, which possibly begins with an offering formula addressed to Osiris. Unfortunately, the second like, which would have contained the name of the deceased, is unreadable. The condition of the stela is relatively poor, which has been blackened by dirt and grime. The decoration of the stela fits best with Type Abydos II G of Munro's classification, which come from the cemetery of Abydos and date to the sixth century BC.

sf:b461baf4969745d0b0ab7117d556b4e5.d: Latin verse inscription in highlighted red letters on grey sandstone recording the visit of Mamertinus, Roman governor of Egypt, to the singing statue of Memnon at Thebes. The author praises the piety of the age of Hadrian which caused the statue to sing. Made by [Daniel Pett](https://sketchfab.com/danielpett) from 37 OnePlus3 mobile phone photographs. This is attached to the wall in gallery 70, so the reverse and base is not visible fully for photogrammetry. COL: [GAA1852](https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/G_1973-0107-1)

sf:b511b0889a014430b2252f6f68880ebe.d: A wooden funerary stela, which dates to the Ptolemaic Period (c. 332–30 BC). It contains painted decoration on the front face. The upper register shows the winged sun disc representing Horus of Edfu (Behdety). Two uraei hang down from the sun disc, each of whom wears the Red Crown (right) and White Crown (left). Between the uraei are the rays of the sun, which are painted red. The upper scene is separated from the central one by the sign for the sky. In this register, the deceased is depicted on the right with his hands raised in adoration before Re and Osiris. A large table of offerings is located between the deceased and the deities, both of whom are represented seated. Re has the head of a falcon and holds an ankh and was-sceptre. Osiris wears the Atef Crown and also holds an ankh and was-sceptre. The final register contains four rows of hieroglyphs painted black, which begin with the offering formula to Re-Horakhty. The inscription identifies the owner as Pamenes, the son of Herefernit and Satweret.

sf:bce70786aead412693b7bca967142099.d: Roman neck ring with inscription. The neck ring shows a piston-shaped enlargement and a cut-out hole of identical shape at the left end. The rims of the obverse are lined with short notches and small punched circles as well as cube eyes in the area of the thickening. Stamped inscription FELICES TVN(GRI) on the obverse and name VRBICVS incised in cursive on the reverse. Torques, originally the neck rings of Celtic warriors, are documented as military awards in the Roman army since Republican times and were usually worn over the breast on the armour. Golden neck rings are also mentioned as a common accoutrement of the draconiarii, the bearers of the Draco standard, which was used as a cohort field sign until late antiquity. The inscription FELICES TUN(GRI) probably refers to the auxiliary unit of the Sagittarii Tungri mentioned in the Notitia dignitatum. It is therefore probably the only military insignia of a standard bearer known at present. Gold; l 8,5 cm; w 1,2–2,4 cm; early 4th century AD.

sf:be42054fe8b64c0c8c8ed27c3953aa63.d: Cuneiform on clay tablet. Cuneiform is the world's oldest known written language developed by the ancient Sumerians of Mesopotamia in the 4th millennium BC. The inscriptions were made with reed styluses to impress some 900 different logographic, syllabic and taxographic signs into moist clay tablets. The text dates from the third dynasty of Ur (Ur III, c. 2100-2000 BC). The original text that was impressed on the tablet has, for the most part, been rendered illegible by a seal that was stamped over the surface. The seal appears to have belonged to Shara-bazige, a scribe who was employed by Ur-Lisi, governor of Umma, a city-state in southern Mesopotamia and a key center during the Ur III period. This particular seal has been identified on several other Ur III texts.

sf:bfa05fa9b503442cb689a0325e7bfde3.d: **Interlace stone fragment with ogham inscription, Whiteness, Shetland, Scotland, UK** Portion of a slab of red sandstone, sculptured on one side, from St Ola’s Church, Whiteness, Shetland. An adjoining fragment of the same stone was found separately and now resides in Shetland Museum, Lerwick (ARC 8057). The left hand frame contains a fragment of the ogham inscription which would have run around the edge of the stone. sf:bfc0c0381c5c437fbe3f0b94257c1b9f.d: Roman, 1st-2nd centuries AD From Halikarnassos (modern Bodrum), Turkey This marble sculpture, carved in relief, commemorates the honourable release from service (missio) of two women fighters, 'Amazon' (named after the fierce female warriors) and 'Achilia' (after the Greek hero Achilles). They are shown with the same equipment as their male counterparts, swords and shields, but without helmets - perhaps to emphasize their female hairstyles. This scene, together with the inscription APELUTHESAN, "they were freed", indicates that they won their freedom after a series of outstanding performances. Heads of spectators of their fight can be seen on either side of the platform they are standing on. According to several contemporary eye-witnesses, women often performed as gladiators in the Roman arena. According to the biographer Suetonius, the emperor Domitian (AD 81-96) even made women fight by torchlight at night. Formerly in the collection of Viscount Stratford de Redcliffe GR 1847.4-24.19 (Sculpture 1117)

sf:bffc52dbce7148069264ea7ba6d86fc0.d: The epigraph is located in the atrium of the municipal building of the city of terracina, Italy The inscription in Latin is: P(ublius) Numisius P(ubli) f(ilius) Ouf(entina) Iacul[a IIvir] / iter(um) praef(ectus) pro IIv[iro] / P(ublius) Numisius P(ubli) f(ilius) Ouf(entina) Festus [---] / Pantuleia / P(ublius) Numisius P(ubli) l(ibertus) Ter[tius]. The epigraph shows the name of the freedman Publius Numisius Tertius of the gens Numisia. Before him two deceased, of free status belonging to the same gens, are mentioned. The first was Publius Numisius Iacula, son of Publius of the Oufentina tribe, and Publius Numisius Festus of the same tribe of Iacula (they were probably brothers because they have the same patronymic.) Tertius was perhaps freedman of their father). Iacula was twice duumvir (IIvir), and praefectus pro duumviro, that is to say he replaced one of the two duumvirs in office due to impediments of the latter or for other reasons. The inscription is incomplete in some points.

sf:c4afb8c547924490bf1a8766b58b1890.n: Epitafio de Cayo Atilio Áquilo (siglo I d. C.)
sf:c4afb8c547924490bf1a8766b58b1890.d: Encaje de dos fragmentos epigráficos que obraron juntos en un monumento dedicado a _C. Atilius Aquilus_ por _Cornelia Placida_. La parte izquierda puede verse en el exterior del torreón de Sofuentes, mientras que la derecha está reutilizada en el interior de un domicilio anejo. Probablemente, sería el elemento central de un monumento funerario con relieve de armas cuyos restos aún pueden verse. Fechada en el siglo I d. C., atestigua el arraigo de los _Atilii_ en la zona. Two joining fragments -found separately- of the inscription from a monument dedicated to _C. Atilius Aquilus_ by _Cornelia Placida_. The left side was reused to build the external wall of the medieval tower at Sofuentes (Zaragoza, Spain). The right fragment was reused at a private property beside the tower. It was probably at the centre of a majestic funerary monument with armours. It can be dated to the 1st century AD and interpreted as a symbol of the power of the _Atilii_ in the area. Dimensiones (cm): a) 66 x (40) x ?. b) 66 x 38 x ?.

Guadalajara: Diputación Provincial. **Acknowledgment**: This work is part of the collaboration agreement signed in 2020 between the Junta de Comunidades de Castilla-La Mancha and Global Digital Heritage for the digitization of the Cultural Heritage of Castilla-La Mancha region. We want to publicly thank the collaboration of the Museum of Guadalajara, especially by its director Fernando Aguado and its curator Miguel Ángel Cuadrado.

sf:c495f3b78af24aeca508efd7344b6486.d: Miliario del emperador Augusto, con alusión a la *legio X Gemina*, una de las tres que intervinieron en la pavimentación y apertura de la denominada "vía romana de las Cinco Villas" que enlazaba, desde la fundación de *Caesar Augusta* (Zaragoza), esta ciudad con *Pompelo* (Pamplona) enlazando el valle del Ebro con el Pirineo. Fue hallado entre Ejea de los Caballeros y Castejón de Valdejasa, en la zona de los montes de Sora. Milestone of Emperor Augustus mentioning the *Legio X Gemina*, one of the three Augustan legions that took part to the paving of the so-called “Roman road of the Cinco Villas” that since its foundation linked *Caesar Augusta* (Zaragoza) with *Pompelo* (Pamplona), connecting the Ebro valley with the Pyrenees. It was found between Ejea de los Caballeros and Castejón de Valdejasa, in the area of the mounts of Sora. Dimensiones (cm): 206 x 53

sf:c674400ae40d4e3991bfc477d674b42c.n: Epitafio de Atilio Materno (siglo II d.C.)
sf:c674400ae40d4e3991bfc477d674b42c.d: Inscripción funeraria romana reutilizada en uno de los contrafuertes de la parroquia de Malpica de Arba, en el término municipal de Biota, dedicada a Nuestra Señora de Diasol y que fue descubierta en los años 90 del siglo XX. Debe proceder del entorno, donde no faltan yacimientos romanos del tipo _uillae_. Formaría parte del epitafio de _Atilius Maternus_ que porta un gentilicio común en la zona y de clara relación con Los Bañales. Roman funerary inscription reused in the buttress of the Church of Malpica de Arba (Biota) dedicated to Our Lady of Diasol. The inscription was found in the 1990s and it must come from de surroundings of Biota, where several Roman sites such as _uillae_ have been found. It might belong to the epitaph of _Atilius Maternus_, a gentilicium common in the area and related to the city of Los Bañales.

sf:cac1bde53bf744ee91ca08af2cb9f800.d: Important preserved archaeological find in Terracina (iTaly) at the Filosi Professional Institute. "The decree of the Pontiffs" are two Roman-era piers that belonged to it to an ancient portal that probably introduced into a religious sepulchral area. The inscription placed on them is dated between 101 AD and 250 d.C. Very rare and it is basically about authorizations that were issued to requesting persons for the arrangement of a sepulcher. The rarity of this artifact is also in the formula used in the inscription which also recalls propitiatory sacrifices. In fact, before rebuilding in this case the funeral monument would have had to sacrifice a sheep dark color that would have been a good omen to cleanse the area sepulchral.

sf:cc588f678717414099658cf485004d81.d: Milestone from the site of El Morell (Tarragona, Spain), dated in the 3rd century AD. Found in El Morell, 15km from Tarragona, on the ancient road from Tarragona to Lleida. The inscription, wich is incomplete, refers to the restoration carried out by Publius Portus on the road that led from Tarraco to Ilerda in time of Valerian and Gallienus. The Romans placed these mile-stones on the most important communications routes to show the distance in miles between the specific place and the city of Rome. 1206 photos completely processed in Reality Capture. The project was done with the support of the National Archaeological Museum of Tarragona and the Agència Catalana del Patrimoni Cultural. Catalog No. MNAT 37246. Museu Nacional Arqueològic de Tarragona (2019): Tarraco: Exposición de síntesis. Generalitat de Catalunya Publicacions.

sf:cc61017f2d2642e39f1e55d907dde000.d: A Near Eastern stamp seal inscribed with a personal or clan device, described as a 'fire altar' by Myres (1914). Dating to the 3rd–7th century CE, the seal comes from the Neo-Persian Empire which encompassed modern-day Iran, Iraq, and Afghanistan among others. The design consists of a crescent, standard, bar with terminals twice occuring, and ribbons tied at the bottom. These abstract insignia may have been highly prized, and the seals bearing them were probably used by numerous members, dependents, and servants of a particular clan or estate. A similar example can be found in the [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/321489?searchField=All&sortBy=Relevance&ft=Sasanian+stamp+seal&offset=80&rpp=80&pos=123) (accession number 74.51.4411 ) see also (Brunner, 1978: 126, no. 83). Accession Number: RWH 185 Photography and Model Credit: Charlotte Sargent

sf:ccbe2e02eec74504866e93b26c4516bd.d: Roman marble funerary monument dated in the 3rd century A.D. It belonged to Lucius Julius Polybius as the inscription of four lines that still retains on one of its faces and in which we can read: D(is). M(anibus). S(acrum) L(ucius). I(ulius). POLIBIVS ANN(orum). LXXII (septuaginta duorum) H(ic). S(itus). E(st). S(it). T(ibi). T(erra). L(evis). The translation according to Encarnação, (1984) would say: “Consecrated to the Manes gods. Here lies Lucius Julius Polybius, seventy-two years old. May the earth be light to you”. The funerary monument is of the Cupa type, named for its characteristic cylindrical shape that mimics a lying tank (Cupa means barrel in Latin). It is currently preserved in the Frei Manuel do Cenáculo National Museum (Évora, Portugal). Catalog No. ME1723. ENCARNAÇÃO, José d' - IRCP - Inscrições Romanas do Conventus Pacensis - Subsídios para o estudo da romanização. Coimbra: Inst. Arqueolog. Fac. Letras, 1984, p. 380. 598 photos from Canon 5D Mk IV. Completely processed in Reality Capture.

sf:ce75bd8464f747338c0252f0c1dcc57e.d: On the ancient Appian way to Terracina (Italy) and, on the left of the ancient road, lies a Roman funerary epigraph. The same is unattended and has been the subject of at least three attempts of proven theft (so I have reported the residents in the area). Datable between 50 BC / 50 d.C. the Latin text reads: [- A] tinius ((mulieris)) l (ibertus) Priamus; [- A] tinius C (ai) f (ilius) Rufus f (ilius); [- A] tinius C (ai) f (ilius) Proculus f (ilius) [sibi et libe] ris libert (is) que eorum. Bibliography: Bulletin of the Institute of History and Art of Southern Lazio, 8, 2, 1975, pp. 23-27, with photos (U. Broccoli) - AE 1978 (1) AE 1978, 0075 (2) HD013023 (H. Niquet) (3)

sf:cf67bd47903a4a8cb9b6586bacb7d68c.d: This medieval inscription (38 x 21 cm) located in the cathedral of Sigüenza (Spain) says: VITALIS : VITA : SUBLACTUS : SORTE : LEVITA : PRIMUS : IN : HOC : ATRIO : CLAUDITUR : HOSPICIO : ERA : MILLESIMA : DUCENTESIMA : TRICESIMA : PBR : HUNC : SEQUITUR : W. : ET : HIC : SEPELITUR : Vital, por suerte levita, arrebatado de la vida, es el primero que en este claustro recibe albergue en la era 1230 (1192 d.C.). A este le sigue el presbítero W. y aquí esta sepultado. 3D model made in Reality Capture using 200 images with additional processing completed in Geomagic Wrap. This work is part of the collaboration agreement signed in 2020 between the Junta de Comunidades de Castilla-La Mancha and Global Digital Heritage. We want to thank the Bishopric of Sigüenza-Guadalajara and the cathedral chapter, especially D. Jesús de las Heras, D. Miguel Ángel Ortega and D. sf:d0b53a80ebd545a6abe8ad5f23a5ebca.d: This sandstone idol was originally placed in a niche inside a temple. It depicts a stylized face in the Arabian style of Nabataean art. The Nabataean inscription on the base notes who is represented: goddess of Hayyan son of Nayibat. Raqmu-Petra, Temple of the Winged Lions. Nabataean (early 1st century AD). JP13483 . This project was a collaboration between the PDTRA, DoA, GDH, and ACOR. Scanned by GDH in November 2024 using Leo Artec.

sf:d7ea4fa8567448c79e01f0c5db56ef8c.d: A large fragment of a round-topped donation stela of sandstone. The winged disc representing Horus of Behdet (Behdety) is depicted in the lunette. Emanating from the sun disc are two uraei, who wear the White Crown (left) and Red Crown (right). An inscription between them reads "Behdety, the Great God, Lord of the Sky". A pt (sky) sign separates the lunette from the scene below. In this scene, the ruler is depicted on the right side making a donation to a procession of deities. He wears the Double Crown with an uraeus at the front. The cartouches above read pr-ꜥꜣ (Pharaoh) rather than giving the name of the ruler. The procession of gods consists of Montu-Re, Montu-Re-Horakhty, Tjenenet-Iunit, and Raettawy. Both forms of Montu hold a was-sceptre and wear a headdress consisting of double plumes and sun disc. Both have a double uraeus on their forehead. Tjenenet-Iunit wears the Double Crown while holding a papyrus staff, while Raettawy has a headdress consisting of cow horns and a sun disc.

sf:d8a3d415fd764471af8f95895f08c0a8.d: Amulet of the lion-headed goddess Bastet in faience. The goddess has a mane and a tripartite wig. There is a uraeus on the top of her head, which continues into a suspension loop at the back. She is in a striding pose with the right arm at the side while the left one is holding a wadjet eye on the chest. There is a plinth at the bottom. The back pillar carries the hieroglyphic inscription identifying the goddess: ‘Words spoken by Bastet’. The corner of the base is chipped. Previously part of the Ogden collection, which was gifted to Harrogate Museum in the 1930s. Bastet was the feline goddess of female sexuality, pregnant women, and children.

sf:d9c53ae66e9946fbb7b68fa336de1b87.n: Miliario de Treboniano Galo (251-253 d. C.)
sf:d9c53ae66e9946fbb7b68fa336de1b87.d: Fragmento de la parte superior de un miliario de arenisca local que fuera hallado por el vecino de Layana, Luis Pueyo, en las proximidades de la localidad que da hoy acceso al yacimiento, en concreto en el término de La Estanca/La Portillala, al Oeste de Layana. Formaría parte de los miliarios de la vía _Caesar Augusta-Summum Pyrenaeum_ y se fecharía ya en el siglo III d. C. Se conserva en el Museo de Zaragoza. Fragment of the upper side of a milestone in local sandstone found by Luis Pueyo near Layana, the town through which we access the archaeological site of Los Bañales today. The stone lied just outside of La Estanca/La Portillala, west of Layana. It is one of the milestones of the road _Caesar Augusta - Summum Pyrenaeum_ and it can be dated to the 3rd century AD. It is now preserved in the Museum of Zaragoza. Dimensiones (cm): 41 x 45

sf:d45c656d5376476ea4e35b60d4d59533.d: An irregular limestone stela, which dates from the Byzantine Period of Egypt (c. fourth to seventh centuries AD). The obverse surface features a deeply incised inscription arranged in at least nine horizontal lines, written in Coptic. Despite some minor surface wear and irregular breaks along the edges of the stone, the text remains legible, preserving standard funerary phrasing dedicated to a monk named Mêna, who belonged to the topos of the venerable Apollô (potentially Bāwīṭ, though other monastic sites are attested). Spelling features point toward Middle Egypt, and Mêna's day of repose is recorded as the tenth of Mešir (corresponding to February 4th or 5th depending on leap years). The reverse side is rough-hewn with visible chisel marks, indicating that the stone was originally embedded into a wall or architectural structure.

sf:d93269013cab473e9b1fab434e0710ce.d: Roomalainen hopearaha, denaari. Etusivulla on Roman pää, katse oikealle suunnattuna. Vasemmassa laidassa seppele ja alapuolella teksti ROMA. Takasivulla on kahden hevosen vetämässä sotavaunussa seisova Victoria. Oikeassa laidassa maissintähkä ja alla kolikon lyöttäjän tunnus T. CLOVLI. Noin 110 eaa. Roman silver coin, denarius. The front of the coin features the helmeted head of Rome. On the left side of the head is a wreath and below the inscription ROMA. The back of the coin features Victory in a two-horse chariot (biga). A corn-ear in the right corner and below the inscription of the moneyer T.CLOVLI. Ca. 110 BCE. 3D-digitoitu osana Kotona kulttuurissa -tutkimushanketta 2020-2021, käyttäen digitaalista fotogrammetriaa. 3D-digitointia on yksinkertaistettu huomattavasti katselukokemuksen sujuvoittamiseksi. 3D digitized as part of the Making Home Abroad research project 2020-2021, using digital photogrammetry. sf:e2f68764376543a8893063ce6eaf1829.d: Miliario opistógrafo de arenisca con inscripción en ambos lados y correspondiente al reinado del emperador Tiberio. Según su descubridor fue hallado cerca del corral de Baranguán, en las cercanías de Sádaba (Zaragoza) pero camino ya -por El Espartal- de Santacara (Navarra). Serviría a la bifurcación de la vía *Caesaraugusta-Pompelo* hacia *Cara* (Santacara) atestiguada desde época tiberiana. Fue depositado en el Museo de Zaragoza en enero de 2019. Sandstone milestone inscribed on both sides dated to the reign of Emperor Tiberius. According to its finder, it was found by the Corral de Barangúan, near Sádaba (Zaragoza), on the way to Santacara (Navarra) following the way of El Espartal. It would have served the junction on the via *Caesarausta-Pompelo* in the direction of *Cara* (Santacara), which is attested from the Tiberian period. It was deposited at Museo de Zaragoza in January, 2019. Dimensiones (cm): (173) x 57 diam.

sf:e97f95d5781a4359b5a744b0cf0328fa.n: Votive stele - Buddha and two Bodhisattvas
sf:e97f95d5781a4359b5a744b0cf0328fa.d: Buddhist votive stele with Buddha and two Bodhisattvas, 678 CE, now at Mia. From [artsmia.org](www.artsmia.org): *'This stone stele depicts the Buddha sitting on a lotus throne, flanked by a pair of bodhisattvas. His left hand is raised in abhaya mudra (gesture of dispelling fear), and the right is resting on his knee. The figures in this stele illustrate the vivid and naturalistic qualities that are characteristic of Buddhist icons of the Tang dynasty ... The inscription tells us that the stele was commissioned during the reign of Emperor Gaozong in 678, and remarkably lists both the Emperor and the Empress, Wu, as beneficiaries. It was highly unusual for an empress to be included in this way prior to this time, proving her rising power before ultimately becoming the most powerful woman in the Tang dynasty when she became the de facto ruler of China in 690.'* More information [here](https://collections.artsmia.org/art/140016/buddhist-votive-stele-with-buddha-and-two-bodhisattvas-china)

sf:e677abb406b94c909ebea39deb24675f.d: Walking in Terracina (Italy) in Piazza Municipio means reliving the atmospheres of a true Roman forum. The stone paving, dating back to the Augustea age, is still intact and along its original central axis the inscription “A. Aemilius Auli f. stravit “, or” Aulus Emilio, son of Aulus, has paved “. A kind of signing, in short, the Roman magistrate who financed the paving of the forum. It is bordered to the north by a paved tract in a different way: it is of the ancient Appian Way, which cut the city in all its length and that after the square it goes to disappear under the medieval buildings.

sf:ea240a75426f413ab6c7686862a930eb.d: Egyptian, Middle Kingdom, late Dynasty 12-early Dynasty 13, ca. 1879-1778 BCE Excavated at the Temple of Osiris at Abydos Black granite Lent to the Yale Are Gallery by the Peabody Museum, Yale University, ANT 006640 An inscription on the back identifies this statue as an offering to Osiris, god of the afterlife. sf:ec32f9a5550f4d3589e58ed6c267d28a.d: An irregularly shaped limestone stela with a rough, jagged outline, whose front surface features a deeply incised and poorly preserved raised relief carving. The scene depicts two people facing right: a soldier at the front holding a bow in his left hand and a sheaf of arrows in his right, and wearing a broad collar; and behind him, a woman in a long dress with her left arm raised towards the man's head in a gesture of affection or protection. The decoration is executed in a crudely cut style, and faint traces of hieroglyphs are visible above the woman's head. The reverse side is rough and undecorated. This type of stela, known as a "soldier stela", is characteristic of the First Intermediate Period (c. 2181–2055 BC). Purchased by Sir Henry Wellcome in 1906 from the collection of Robert de Rustafjaell. On long-term loan to the Egypt Centre since 1971 as part of the dispersal of the Wellcome collection.

sf:ed9b87c8df9340b4ba691ddc2a8e7daf.n: Funerary inscription of the Spurius family
sf:ed9b87c8df9340b4ba691ddc2a8e7daf.d: Funerary inscription of the Spurius family. Roman, 2nd century BCE. Marble, pigment; 35 x 34.5 x 8 cm. ID: 0000.00.1037. This tombstone for the Spurius family is a rare example of a Republican-period inscription from the Bay of Naples, but it shows some facets that became standardized in later tombstones. The grouping of relatives together in a large tomb was a common practice to demonstrate the family’s wealth, especially if it was in a prominent location. Intriguingly, this inscription was carved on a re-used column base, one of numerous examples of the re-use of building materials for inscriptions and vice-versa. Translation: "Gnaeus Spurius, the son of Ovus; Singullia, the daughter of Marcus; Marcus Spurius, the son of Gnaeus; Gnaeus Spurius, the son of Gnaeus Frugus." For more info and links to raw data, see: https://quod.lib.umich.edu/k/kelsey/x-0000.00.1037

sf:efa0fa04da23480f82baa263d54858ee.un: Harvard Museum of the Ancient Near East
sf:efa0fa04da23480f82baa263d54858ee.d: Headrest New Kingdom Wood Possibly from Illahun Harvard Semitic Museum 1902.17.7 The inscription on column of headrest, starts with “the good god” then a break over what was a cartouche, and ends with “given life.” The cartouche has enough space and traces of inscription to accommodate three or four signs. The last sign appears to be a neb basket, with a seated deity over it (Amenhotep III? Ramses IV?). There is also a (secondarily carved?) sa sign carved on one side of the base, the word for “son” or the god Geb. wear pattern on the cartouche suggests it was grabbed frequently around the post of the headrest, the object may have been used in life and then deposited in a burial. References: Flinders Petrie, Objects of Daily Use (London, 1927), p. 35 no. 32 and pl. XXXII no. 32. Also Lexikon der Ägyptologie III, 690, and illustration p. 687, no. 9 from Gurob. *Scanned by Andréa Martinez with the Artec Spider 3D Scanner*

sf:f2ab7074a5ec4eaea432866ae8a9ff88.n: Altar de la Victoria imperial (siglo I d. C.)
sf:f2ab7074a5ec4eaea432866ae8a9ff88.d: Mitad superior de un altar cilíndrico en arensica, con _foculus_ en su coronamiento y con texto sólo en la cara frontal. La pieza fue extraída en el otoño de 2013 por una tormenta y recogida en la ermita de Nuestra Señora de Los Bañales. Revisando material en estudio, fue descubierto su texto en abril de 2018. Se conserva en la nave municipal del Ayuntamiento de Layana. Podría fecharse a finales del siglo I d. C. Half part of a cylindric altar made of local sandstone, with _foculus_ in its upper part, and with text on the front. The altar was found in the autum of 2013 because of a storm and was then preserved in the chapel of Our Lady of Los Bañales. Its text was discovered in April 2018. Now it is preserved in Layana's municipal depot. It could be dated to the end of Ist century AD.

sf:f7bbea2b91d54f5f8b71c3ad316aa770.d: Paulo's funeral tombstone dated 544 A.D. possibly from Mértola. It is carved on a large rectangular slate plate. It has an incised decoration with two columns, a Greek cross and two rosettes. Keep an inscription: DEPOSI / TIO PAV / LI FAMV / LVS DEI / VIXSIT / ANNOS L E / T VNO REQUI / EVIT IN PAC / E D (ie) III IDVS M / ARTIAS R / A DLXXXII. The translation would be: Deposition of Paulo, servant of God. He lived 51 years. He rested in peace on the 3rd day of the idus of March of the 582 era (March 13, 544). It is currently preserved in the Frei Manuel do Cenáculo National Museum (Évora, Portugal). Catalog No. ME1725. BARATA, António Francisco - Catalogo do Museu Archeologico da Cidade de Evora. Lisboa: Imprensa Nacional, 1903, p. 39. VIVES, José - Inscripciones Cristanas de la España Romana y Visigoda. Barcelona: 1969, p. 83. 316 photos from Canon 5D Mk IV. Completely processed (aligned, scaled, meshed, cleaned, simplified, unwrapped, textured) in Reality Capture.

sf:f975e1e56d6744cfb5963367b0160253.d: A complete mummiform wooden shabti dating to the late Eighteenth Dynasty (c. 1400–1300 BC), inscribed for the scribe Nedjem. The figure is carved from wood, with its arms crossed right over left across the chest. Little of the original paint remains across the darkened wooden surface, except for seven rows of black hieroglyphs on the front that record Chapter 6 of the Book of the Dead (the "shabti spell"). Notably, the face and hands contain traces of ancient gilding, adding a costly and reflective element to the facial features and crossed fists. A deep, natural vertical split in the wood runs down the entire left side of the figure, with another significant fissure extending down the centre of the reverse.

sf:f1828f935e8d47d6933f00d8cafb4720.d: Fragment of inscription of a chief magistrate. Roman, Flavian (69–96 CE). Marble, plaster, pigment; 21 x 18.7 x 3.7 cm. ID: 0000.00.0818d. Portion of a monumental public inscription preserving one letter and an interpunct (a dot separating letters and/or words in ancient inscriptions). The edge to the left of the "A." is straight and the back shows possible traces of attachment, suggesting that it is the beginning of the entire inscription. This would leave the "A." standing on its own, suggesting it may be part of a name: "A." was the standard abbreviation of "Aulus", a common Roman praenomen (given/first name). The break on this stone connects with other pieces in our collection, helping to confirm our reading of this fragment. Full inscription: * Latin: *A(ulus) Caeci(lius Ru)fus II vir.* * Translation: "Aulus Caecilius Rufus, the chief magistrate (*duumvir*)." For more info and links to raw data, see: https://quod.lib.umich.edu/k/kelsey/x-0000.00.0818d

sf:f14466adf0c647f48d57a5e96b7696f9.d: This limestone altar has 6 lines of Latin inscribed on two sides. The text mentions Marcus Aurelius Antoninus. (M.AVR. ANTONI), the Roman Emperor from AD 161 to 180. After the annexation of the Nabataean Kingdom into the Roman Empire, Latin - the official language of the Roman Empire - was used in Petra alongside the local Nabataean; Greek also continued to be used. Latin was used for official monument, milestones of the Via Nova Traina and tomb inscriptions of the Romans, like the Latin inscription of the Sextius Florentinus Tomb. This altar was possibly used by the Roman official in Petra. Roman period (AD 161-180). JP6493. This project was a collaboration between the PDTRA, DoA, GDH, and ACOR. Scanned by GDH in November 2024 using Leo Artec scanner.

sf:fbbf72c144da4eec85fbb66cf2800b83.d: Roman tombstone / Stela with figural decoration and inscription. From Hardomlje near Ljubuški, Bosnia and Herzegovina. Curated in the National Museum, Sarajevo. Data were collected as part of a joint research project between GDH and the Association for the Digitization and Informatisation of Cultural Heritage (DIGI.BA) in Sarajevo, in full collaboration with the National Museum of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sarajevo. sf:fbdbac87b671468ebea9fc8f2166482a.n: Funerary inscription of a Praetorian officer
sf:fbdbac87b671468ebea9fc8f2166482a.d: Funerary inscription of Lucius Calpurnius Rufus. Roman, 71–214 CE. Marble; 29 x 38 x 2.6 cm. ID: 0000.00.0878. The Praetorian fleet at Misenum was founded by Augustus in 27 BCE and protected the western Mediterranean from piracy and other naval threats. Lucius Calpurnius Rufus was a scriba—an administrative role within the navy that would serve as a ship or squadron’s clerk—for this fleet. This inscription was set up in Italy, even though he passed away and was buried in Ephesus (Türkiye). This inscription was written on the back of a reused fragment of a monumental inscription, probably Augustan in date. Translation: "To the Shades of the Underworld: for Lucius Calpurnius Rufus, an officer (scriba) of the Praetorian fleet of Misenum. This man, sent to Ephesus on duty, died and was laid there in a marble sarcophagus. Marcus Sittius Africanus, his fellow countryman and heir, made this memorial at the camp." For more info and links to raw data, see: https://quod.lib.umich.edu/k/kelsey/x-0000.00.0878

sf:fc6e15d6b898497ab40a47f0b5002c87.d: An ancient Egyptian stela (typically a stone slab bearing a commemorative inscription or relief design) dedicated to a man called Neferemshety or Neferempet (reading is unclear). Neferemshety holds a staff of authority in one hand, and a sceptre in the other. The inscription is an example of the ‘offering formula’ which guarantees offerings for the deceased in the afterlife. Underneath the inscription is an offering table. On top of it is a leg of beef and a trussed fowl. Beside the table is the head of a cow, over an oval shape that represents a loaf of bread. To the right is a beer jug (sitting in a jar stand – an essential bit of furniture when jars had pointy bottoms). The offering formula often specifies these four offerings, ‘bread, beer, oxen and fowl’. You can read more about this object [here](https://garstangmuseum.wordpress.com/2020/11/09/stela-of-neferemshety-garstang-museum-e-88/). Accession Number: E.88 Description Credit: Roland Enmarch Photography and Model Credit: Charlotte Sargent

sf:fe57fcbfa3454b7c9b13f04352752f91.d: Q. Titiuksen lyöttämä hopeadenaari. Etusivulla viinin, juhlimisen ja vapauden jumala Liber / Bacchus. Takasivulla Pegasus, alla Titiuksen tunnus "Q. TITI". Rooman valtakunta, noin 90 eaa. Silver denarius from the time of the republican moneyer Q. Titius. Obverse side: Liber / Bacchus, the God of wine, viticulture and freedom, looking to the right, with a wreath of wine leafs on his hair. Reverse side: A pegasus and the inscription of Titius "Q. TITI". Ancient Rome, circa 90 BCE. 3D-digitoitu osana Making Home Abroad / Kotona kulttuurissa -tutkimushanketta 2020-2021, käyttäen digitaalista fotogrammetriaa. 3D-digitointia on yksinkertaistettu huomattavasti katselukokemuksen sujuvoittamiseksi. 3D digitized as part of the Making Home Abroad / Kotona kulttuurissa research project 2020-2021, using digital photogrammetry. The 3D digitization is strongly simplified to ensure a smooth online visualization.
